### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the adaptation of software for debugging purposes was provided for through an exception to copyright infringement inserted into **Section 52(1)** of the Copyright Act, 1957, complemented by a protective proviso in **Section 57** regarding author's special rights [3][30][44].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Instrument:** The Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992 (amending the Copyright Act, 1957) [2].
* **Status:** Legislative proposal as introduced / amended in Parliament; not law in force in that specific bill form [2].
* **Ministry / Desk Context:** Introduced under the Ministry of Human Resource Development (Statement signed by Minister Arjun Singh on 6 May 1992) [15].

### DESIGN & STATUTORY PROVISIONS
The Bill addressed software adaptation and debugging through two coordinated statutory mechanisms:

1. **Insertion of Section 52(1)(aa):**
   * **Clause 17(3)** of the Bill proposed to insert clause **(aa)** into sub-section (1) of Section 52 of the principal Act [44].
   * It declared that the following acts would not constitute an infringement of copyright:
     > *"(aa) the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
     > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
     > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [44]
   * As explained in the **Notes on Clauses** (Clause 17), this new clause was introduced to *"cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for 'debugging' and to make back-up copies"* while explicitly excluding computer programmes from general private-use copying exemptions under Section 52(1)(a) [3].

2. **Consequential Proviso to Section 57 (Author's Special Rights):**
   * **Clause 20** of the Bill substituted Section 57(1) of the principal Act and added a specific proviso limiting the author's moral rights/special rights against modification or distortion [30][49]:
     > *"Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies."* [49]
   * The Notes on Clauses confirmed that this proviso was added in respect of computer programmes consistent with the proposal in Section 52(1)(aa), *"whereby adaptation of a computer programme for the purpose commonly known as 'debugging' is sought to be made permissible"* without exposure to restraint or damages from the author [30].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Enables lawful possessors and bona fide users of software to fix defects, debug, configure, and maintain operation for the intended purpose without committing copyright infringement or facing author moral-rights claims [3][30].
* **Case Against / Restraints:** Narrowed general "private study" fair-dealing exemptions by expressly excluding computer programmes from Section 52(1)(a) to protect copyright holders against unauthorized domestic copying [3][44].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* Check how these provisions were subsequently enacted into the Copyright Act, 1957 via the Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994, and further amended by the Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1999 (which introduced interoperability exceptions under Section 52(1)(ab)) [45].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the adaptation of software for debugging purposes was provided for by exempting specific acts from copyright infringement under **Section 52(1)** of the Copyright Act, 1957, coupled with a limitation on an author's special moral rights under **Section 57** [2] [3] [8] [17].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry:** Ministry of Human Resource Development (introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri Arjun Singh, Minister of Human Resource Development, on **6 July 1992**) [33].
* **Instrument:** Statutory Bill (amendment legislation) [5].
* **Status:** Proposed legislative amendment text in the 1992 Bill [5].

### DESIGN & STATUTORY PROVISIONS
The proposal to permit software adaptation for debugging was structured across two primary statutory insertions:

1. **Insertion of Section 52(1)(aa):**
   * Clause 17 of the Bill proposed inserting a new **clause (aa)** in sub-section (1) of Section 52 [3] [8].
   * It provided that the following acts would not constitute copyright infringement:
     > *"(aa) the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
     > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
     > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [8].
   * The Notes on Clauses clarify that this was specifically introduced to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner/possessor of a computer programme copy to make adaptations for **"debugging"** and to make back-up copies [3] [7].

2. **Consequential Proviso to Section 57(1) (Moral Rights):**
   * Clause 20 of the Bill proposed substituting sub-section (1) of Section 57 concerning author's special rights [17] [27].
   * To ensure debugging adaptations would not be restrained as distortion or mutilation, a proviso was added:
     > *"Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies."* [2] [17].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Excludes computer programmes from the overly general "private use" exception while legally enabling bona fide lawful possessors to debug, adapt, and run software for supplied operational needs without facing civil infringement claims or moral rights damages [2] [3] [8] [17].
* **Case Against:** Disallows authors from asserting Section 57 restraint or damage claims against adaptations falling under clause (aa), circumscribing the author's moral rights regarding modifications [2] [17].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* Track subsequent statutory enactments, specifically the substitution and numbering adjustments in the final Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994, and the later expansion of inter-operability and testing exceptions under Section 52(1) in the Copyright (Amendment) Bill, 1999 [14].

### WHAT IT IS
Under **The Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the adaptation of software for debugging purposes was enabled by inserting an exception into the non-infringement provisions of the Copyright Act, 1957 [2][3]. The Bill proposed adding a new clause—**clause (aa)**—to sub-section (1) of **section 52**, specifically exempting the making of copies or adaptations of a computer programme by a lawful possessor for legitimate operational needs [3][8].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / In-Charge:** Ministry of Human Resource Development (introduced by Shri Arjun Singh) [33].
* **Instrument Type:** Amending Legislation (Statutory Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha) [5][33].
* **Stage & Date:** Introduced in the Lok Sabha on **6 July 1992** (Notes/SOR dated **6 May 1992**) [29][33].

### DESIGN & STATUTORY PROVISIONS
According to the text of the Bill and the Notes on Clauses:

1. **Insertion of Section 52(1)(aa):**
   Under **Clause 17(3)** of the Bill, a new clause `(aa)` was inserted into section 52(1) to state that the following acts do not constitute an infringement of copyright [8]:
   > *"(aa) the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
   > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
   > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [8]

2. **Debugging Objective:**
   The Notes on Clauses clarify that clause `(aa)` was specifically inserted *"to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for 'debugging' and to make back-up copies"* while excluding computer programmes from the broader *"private study/research"* fair-dealing exemption [3].

3. **Proviso to Section 57 (Author's Special Rights):**
   Under **Clause 20** of the Bill, a corresponding proviso was added to section 57(1) of the principal Act to ensure that the author's moral rights could not override this debugging exception [2][17]:
   > *"Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies."* [2][17]

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Lawful possessors and bona fide users were granted explicit legal protection to debug, adapt, and run software to achieve the intended functionality and maintain backups without risk of civil infringement or criminal penalties [2][3][8].
* **Case Against / Safeguards:** To protect copyright holders against unauthorised leakage, the Bill excluded computer programmes from general *"private use"* copying under section 52(1)(a) and introduced strict penal sanctions under proposed section 63C for the knowing use of infringing copies [3][8][21].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* Check the subsequent legislative enactment via the **Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994**, where section 52(1)(aa) was formally codified into law.

### WHAT IT IS
The Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001 is a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S. S. Ahluwalia [1], [2]. It mandates the provision of free education from school level up to post-graduate and technical education, along with related welfare benefits, to children born of manual scavengers [3].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Jurisdiction / Appropriate Government:** Under Clause 2(a), "appropriate Government" is defined as the State Government in the case of a State, and the Central Government in other cases [4].
* **Status:** Introduced in the Rajya Sabha (Bill No. LXX of 2001); as-introduced text, not enacted into law [4], [1].

### RESPONSIBILITY FOR IDENTIFYING BENEFICIARIES
Under **Clause 3** of the Bill, the identification of eligible beneficiaries is made the statutory duty of the appropriate government through surveys and lists [5]:

* **Duty to Conduct Survey:** The appropriate government must conduct a survey in the area under its jurisdiction to find out the children of scavengers [5].
* **Preparation of List:** It is required to prepare a list of such children who are to be imparted education by the government, drawn up in such manner as may be prescribed by rules [5].
* **Periodic Revision:** The appropriate government is required to cause the list to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [5].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Beneficiary Definition Scope:** Clause 2(e) defines a "scavenger" as a person who had been engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta prior to the commencement of the Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993 [6].
* **Administrative Mechanism:** Clause 7 empowers the appropriate government to appoint Attendance Authorities to monitor attendance and assist in carrying out the purposes of the Bill [7].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Rajya Sabha by **Shri S. S. Ahluwalia** [1, 3]. It aims to provide comprehensive, free educational entitlements to the children of scavengers or Safai Karamcharis who were historically engaged in or employed for manually carrying human excreta [1, 2].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Authority:** The *appropriate Government* is defined as the **State Government** in the case of a State, and the **Central Government** in other cases [1].
* **Form:** Private Member's Bill (Bill No. LXX of 2001) [1].
* **Status:** Introduced in the Rajya Sabha; not enacted law [1].

### IDENTIFICATION RESPONSIBILITY OF THE APPROPRIATE GOVERNMENT
Under **Clause 3** of the Bill (*"Survey to be conducted by the appropriate Government"*), specific statutory identification duties are placed upon the appropriate government [2, 3]:

| Stage / Action | Statutory Requirement (Clause 3) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Survey** | It is the **duty** of the appropriate Government to conduct a survey in the area under its jurisdiction to find out the children of scavengers [2, 3]. |
| **Beneficiary List** | It must prepare a list of such children, in such manner as may be prescribed, who are to be imparted education by such Government [2, 3]. |
| **Revision** | It must cause the list to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [2, 3]. |

### DESIGN & SUPPORTING PROVISIONS
* **Target Group:** Defined as children of a "Scavenger"—namely a person who had been engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta before the commencement of the Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993 [2].
* **Mandatory Entitlements (Clause 4):** Identified beneficiaries are entitled to free education from school level to post-graduate, medical, and technical levels, free hostel facilities, books, uniforms, stationery, transport, and monthly scholarships in deserving cases [3].
* **Enforcement (Clause 7):** The appropriate Government is empowered to appoint **Attendance Authorities** (and assisting officers) to enforce attendance and operationalise educational support [3].
* **Fiscal Requirement:** The Financial Memorandum projects a recurring expenditure of approximately **₹100 crore** per annum and a non-recurring expenditure of **₹10 crore** from the Consolidated Fund of India [2].

### TRADE-OFFS & IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Enforcement Trade-Off:** While Clause 3 mandates state surveys to identify children requiring upliftment [2], Clause 5 places a legal duty directly on scavenger parents to ensure school attendance, and Clause 6 bars persons from employing children if it interferes with schooling [3].
* **Implementation Watch:**
  * Promulgation of rules by the Central Government under Clause 9 specifying the survey methodology, list compilation formats, and revision intervals [2, 4].
  * Demarcation of survey jurisdictions and operational alignment between State Governments and Central agencies [1, 2].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S.S. Ahluwalia [1, 2]. It seeks to eradicate manual scavenging by providing guaranteed free educational facilities—ranging from school to post-graduate, technical, and medical education—to children of scavengers or Safai Karamcharis who were historically engaged in carrying human excreta [1, 3].

### IDENTIFYING ELIGIBLE BENEFICIARIES
Under **Clause 3** ("Survey to be conducted by the appropriate Government") of the Bill, the responsibility assigned to the appropriate government regarding identifying eligible beneficiaries is:

* **Duty to Conduct Survey:** It is the duty of the appropriate Government to conduct a survey within the area under its jurisdiction to find out the children of scavengers [4].
* **Preparation of Beneficiary List:** The appropriate Government must prepare a list, in such manner as may be prescribed by rules, of such children who are to be imparted education by that Government [4].
* **Periodic Revision:** The appropriate Government is mandated to cause this beneficiary list to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [4].

### STATUTORY CONTEXT & DEFINITIONS
* **Appropriate Government:** Defined under Clause 2(a) as the Government of that State in the case of a State, and the Central Government in other cases [1].
* **Beneficiary Qualification:** "Scavenger" is defined under Clause 2(e) as a person who had been engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta before the commencement of the *Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993* [5].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Right to Work Bill, 2002** was introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G. M. Banatwalla to provide a statutory right to work for adult citizens and an unemployment allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) until appropriate work is provided [1, 2]. To finance the allowance and administrative expenditures, the Bill mandates the establishment of the **Right to Work Fund** by the Central Government [3, 4].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ownership:** Administered and established by the Central Government (Ministry of Labour recommendation on record) [1, 3, 5].
* **Status:** Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha; not enacted into law [1, 5].

### DESIGN: MANDATED REVENUE SOURCES OF THE FUND
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Bill, the following five sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [4]:

1. **Government Grants:** All grants made by the Central Government to the Fund from time to time as required under **Section 9(2)** [3, 4].
2. **Voluntary Donations:** All voluntary donations made to the Fund (qualifying for income-tax rebate or deduction under Section 11) [4, 6].
3. **Insurance Policy Contributions:** All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under **Section 10** [3, 4].
4. **Beneficiary Contributions:** All sums collected under **Section 12** (which mandates that every citizen who receives work or allowance under the Act shall contribute to the Fund at a prescribed rate for a prescribed period after securing employment) [4, 7].
5. **Investment Returns:** Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [4].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Rule-Making Requirements:** Prescribing specific contribution rates and durations under Section 12, as well as terms for the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [4, 7, 8].
* **Parliamentary Accountability:** Submission of an annual general report on the working and administration of the Fund before each House of Parliament under Section 14 [9].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Right to Work Bill, 2002** was a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G.M. Banatwalla to provide every eligible unemployed citizen registered at an employment exchange the legal right to work or an unemployment allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) until work is provided [1, 4, 13]. To finance these allowances and the administration of the Act, Section 9 establishes a dedicated **Right to Work Fund** [1, 3].

### MANDATED REVENUE SOURCES CREDITED TO THE FUND
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Bill, the following five sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [1, 3]:

1. **Government Grants:** All grants made by the Central Government to the Fund from time to time as required for the purpose of the Act under Section 9(2) [1, 3].
2. **Voluntary Donations:** All voluntary donations made to the Fund (which qualify for income-tax rebates or deductions under Section 11) [1, 2, 3].
3. **Insurance Contributions:** All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [1, 3].
4. **Beneficiary Contributions:** All sums collected under Section 12, which requires every citizen who receives work or allowance under the Act to contribute to the Fund at a prescribed rate for a prescribed period immediately upon securing work or a job (whether government-provided or secured independently) [1, 3, 21].
5. **Investment Returns:** Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [3].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Right to Work Bill, 2002** was introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G.M. Banatwalla, M.P., to guarantee eligible citizens a legal right to work or an unemployment allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) until appropriate work is provided [1] [2] [3]. To finance the allowance and administrative expenditures, the Bill establishes the **Right to Work Fund** [1] [2].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
- **Proponent / Ministry Context:** Private Member Bill introduced by Shri G.M. Banatwalla, M.P. [3]; received the recommendation of the President under Articles 117(1), 117(3), and 274(1) of the Constitution communicated via the Minister of Labour [4].
- **Legal Status:** Bill as introduced in the Lok Sabha (statutory proposal; not enacted law) [2] [3].

### MANDATED REVENUE SOURCES CREDITED TO THE FUND
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Right to Work Bill, 2002, the following five sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [1] [2]:

| Statutory Clause | Mandated Revenue Source |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Section 9(3)(a)** | All grants made by the Central Government under Section 9(2) (grants made from time to time as required for the purposes of the Act) [1]. |
| **Section 9(3)(b)** | All voluntary donations made to the Fund [1] (which qualify for income-tax rebates or deductions under Section 11) [2]. |
| **Section 9(3)(c)** | All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [1]. |
| **Section 9(3)(d)** | All sums collected under Section 12 (mandatory contributions at a prescribed rate and period from every citizen who receives work or allowance under the Act, payable immediately after securing work) [1] [2] [5]. |
| **Section 9(3)(e)** | Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [2]. |

### TRADE-OFFS
- **Strongest Case For (from record):** Establishes an earmarked multi-source funding model combining central grants, self-sustaining beneficiary contributions upon finding employment, voluntary tax-deductible donations, and insurance backing to progressively reduce pressure on the Consolidated Fund of India [2] [6].
- **Strongest Case Against (from record):** Imposes a recurring charge on the Consolidated Fund of India estimated at approximately ₹500 crore per annum, alongside placing a statutory contribution liability on newly employed individuals under Section 12 [5] [6].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
- **Legislative Progress:** Tracking the passage and debate record of Private Member Bills in the Lok Sabha.
- **Rulemaking Dependencies:** Prescribed contribution rates and periods under Section 12, along with the operational framework of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [1] [5] [7].

Under the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004** (enacted as the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Act, 2007**), the qualifications and criteria for designation as a **recognised security organisation** are defined in newly inserted **Section 344K(f)** of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 [1][17][23].

### Qualifying Criteria
To qualify as a recognised security organisation, an entity must satisfy the following statutory conditions [17][23]:

1. **Form of Entity:** It must be an **organisation, company, firm or body of individuals** [17][23].
2. **Subject-Matter Competence & Qualifications:** It must possess:
   - **Expertise in matters relating to security**, and
   - **Knowledge of ship and port operations** [17][23].
3. **Government Authorisation:** It must be authorised by the **Central Government** by notification in the **Official Gazette** [17][23].
4. **Permitted Scope of Functions:** The authorisation designates the entity to carry out:
   - **Assessment**,
   - **Verification**,
   - **Approval**, or
   - **Certification**
   as required under Part IXB of the Act or by the **International Ship and Port Facility Security Code (ISPS Code)** [17][23].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004** (enacted as the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Act, 2007) [1, 7], a **"recognised security organisation"** is defined under the newly inserted **Section 344K(f)** of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 [2, 3].

### QUALIFICATIONS & DESIGNATION REQUIREMENTS
To qualify and be designated by the Central Government as a recognised security organisation, an entity must satisfy the following statutory requirements [2, 3]:

* **Form of Entity:** It must be an *"organisation, company, firm or body of individuals"* [2, 3].
* **Substantive Expertise & Knowledge:** It must possess:
  * *"expertise in matters relating to security"* [2, 3], and
  * *"knowledge of ship, and port operations"* [2, 3].
* **Official Authorisation:** It must be authorised by the Central Government by **notification in the Official Gazette** [2, 3].
* **Scope of Functions:** The authorisation is to carry out assessment, verification, approval, or certification required under **Part IXB** of the Act or by the **International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code** [2, 3].

### STATUTORY ROLES
Once designated, the Central Government may also authorise a recognised security organisation to carry out security measures (such as setting security levels or providing security information) on its behalf, subject to prescribed conditions under the proviso to **Section 344M(2)** [5].

### **WHAT IT IS**
Under the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004** (enacted as the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Act, 2007) [5, 17], a **"recognised security organisation"** is defined under inserted Section **344K(f)** as any organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals having expertise in matters relating to security and knowledge of ship and port operations [1, 2]. 

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Authority:** Central Government [1, 2].
* **Instrument:** Official notification published in the Official Gazette [2].
* **Statutory Framework:** Part IXB of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 [2, 21].

### **DESIGN & QUALIFYING CRITERIA**
To qualify and be designated by the Central Government, an entity must satisfy the following statutory requirements [1, 2]:

| Dimension | Statutory Requirement |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Entity Form** | Any organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals [1]. |
| **Core Competence** | Expertise in matters relating to security [1]. |
| **Operational Knowledge** | Knowledge of ship and port operations [1]. |
| **Authorised Function** | Authorised by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette to carry out assessment, verification, approval, or certification required by Part IXB or by the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code [2]. |

### **SCOPE OF FUNCTIONS**
* **Delegated Security Measures:** Under the proviso to Section **344M(2)**, the Central Government may authorise any recognised security organisation to carry out security measures on its behalf, subject to prescribed conditions [25].
* **Compliance Framework:** Such bodies assist ships, companies, and port facilities in meeting the mandatory requirements of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) and the ISPS Code [2, 33, 39].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004 (enacted as the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005), the statutory benchmark workday duration for setting piece-rate wage schedules is **seven hours** [1].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Instrument:** The National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004 (subsequently enacted as Act No. 42 of 2005) [2].
* **Statutory Framework:** Governed under **Schedule I, Paragraph 8** (read with Section 4(3) and Section 6) [1, 3].
* **Jurisdiction/Authority:** The State Government fixes the schedule of rates annually in consultation with the State Employment Guarantee Council [4].

### DESIGN
* **Workday Standard:** The schedule of rates of wages for unskilled labourers must be fixed such that an unskilled worker working for **seven hours** would normally earn a wage equal to the statutory daily wage rate [1].
* **Wage Floors:** Under Schedule I, Paragraph 6, labourers cannot be paid less than the statutory wage rate under any circumstances [4]. Section 6 sets a statutory minimum floor of not less than **₹60 per day** [3].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Labor Protection:** Ensures that piece-rate tasks are calibrated to a standard working window (seven hours) to prevent excessive work hours from being required to achieve subsistence daily earnings [1, 4].
* **Implementation Rigidity:** Piece-rate outputs in manual rural public works vary widely across soil types and climatic conditions, making a single schedule calibrated to a seven-hour day difficult to standardize across varied topographies.

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* State Government notifications regarding annual Schedules of Rates (SoRs).
* Alignment of state piece-rate measurements with notified wage rates across rural local bodies.

### WHAT IT IS
Under the statutory framework of the National Rural Employment Guarantee legislation, when wages are directly linked to the quantity of work (piece-rate basis), the schedule of rates fixed by the State Government must be benchmarked against a standard workday of **seven hours** [1], [2]. Specifically, the schedule of rates of wages for unskilled manual labourers must be calibrated such that an individual working for seven hours normally earns an amount equal to the statutory daily wage rate [1], [2].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Authority:** Administered centrally by the Ministry of Rural Development; implemented at the state level by the State Government in consultation with the State Employment Guarantee Council [1], [3].
* **Instrument Type:** Statutory enactment / legislative bill (Schedule I minimum features) [1], [4].
* **Legal Provision:** Paragraph 8, Schedule I (read with Section 4(3) regarding minimum features of rural employment guarantee schemes) [1], [4].

### DESIGN
* **Workday Standard:** Fixed at **seven hours** for the purpose of piece-rate schedule determination [1], [2].
* **Wage Floor Guarantee:** Under no circumstances may workers be paid less than the statutory wage rate, and the rates must ensure that seven hours of standard effort delivers that daily wage rate [1], [2].
* **Periodic Revision:** The schedule of rates must be fixed every year by the State Government in consultation with the State Employment Guarantee Council [1].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Worker Protection (Case For):** Calibrating piece-rate output targets to a standard 7-hour workday prevents excessive physical overexertion and prevents public works authorities from depressing effective daily earnings via inflated physical output quotas [1], [2].
* **Productivity & Measurement (Case Against):** Differing local soil, terrain, and climatic conditions make uniform physical output schedules difficult to standardize across districts without frequent disputes over productivity measurements [1].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Annual Schedule Revisions:** Annual notifications by State Governments reviewing piece-rate schedules alongside the State Council [1].
* **Material vs. Labour Ratio Constraints:** Ensuring that piece-rate project expenditures respect the statutory maximum ceiling of **40%** on the material component (including skilled/semi-skilled wages) [2].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the statutory framework of the National Rural Employment Guarantee legislation, when wages are linked directly to output or the quantity of work done (piece rate), the state's schedule of rates must be calibrated against a standard workday of **seven hours** [1]. * **Statutory Body & Ownership:** The State Government fixes the schedule of rates for different types of work annually, in consultation with the State Employment Guarantee Council [1].
* **Statutory Wage Floor:** Wages paid to labourers under no circumstances may fall below the notified wage rate (initially pegged at not less than **₹60 per day** unless otherwise fixed by the Central Government or aligned with the State's agricultural minimum wage under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948) [1], [3].

| Parameter | Statutory Requirement |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Standard Workday Duration** | **7 hours** [1] |

* **Schedule of Rates (SoR) Revisions:** Annual notifications by State Governments calibrating local task norms (e.g., earth digging, stone-breaking) to the 7-hour standard [1].

Employees have an option to opt out within **six months** from the appointed day, upon which they are deemed to have resigned [9, 11]. Under Clause 8(3), transfer of services entitles no employee to compensation under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 or any other law, and courts or tribunals are barred from entertaining such claims [11]. The Central Government can issue orders to remove difficulties within **two years** from commencement, with every order required to be laid before each House of Parliament (Clause 10) [12].
